unit.title: Segmentation, targeting, positioning
unit.description: STP, segmentation criteria, targeting strategies, positioning statement, perceptual map, jobs to be done

cards.definition: The core method of strategic marketing: split the market into groups with similar needs (Segmentation), choose the groups you will serve (Targeting), then decide the place you want in their mind (Positioning).
cards.example: A running brand splits runners into beginners, marathoners and trail runners, targets trail runners, and positions itself as the grip specialist.
alts: The three-step core of strategic marketing: split the market into groups, choose the groups to serve, then decide the place to win in their minds.

cards.definition: The four families: geographic (country, city, climate), demographic (age, income, job, company size in B2B), psychographic (values, lifestyle) and behavioural (usage, loyalty, benefit sought, purchase moment).
cards.example: Behavioural: heavy users who order every week versus occasional buyers who order twice a year.
alts: The four families used to split a market: where people live, who they are, what they value, and how they buy and use the product.

cards.definition: A useful segment is measurable, large enough to be profitable, reachable through your channels, and it reacts differently from other segments to your offer.
cards.example: Left-handed golfers are measurable, reachable through clubs and forums, and need different equipment: a good segment.
alts: A group of buyers that can be measured, is big enough to pay off, can be reached through your channels and responds to the offer in its own way.

cards.definition: Undifferentiated (one offer for everyone), differentiated (a specific offer per segment), concentrated (one niche, served very well) and micro-marketing (offers tailored to small groups or individuals).
cards.example: A small brand of gluten-free pasta chooses a concentrated strategy instead of fighting Barilla on every shelf.
alts: The choice between one offer for everyone, an offer per group, a single niche served very well, or offers tailored to very small groups.

cards.definition: An internal sentence that fixes the strategy: For (target) who (need), our (brand) is the (category) that (main benefit), unlike (alternative), because (proof).
cards.example: For busy parents who hate meal planning, Quitoque is the meal kit that removes the daily what do we eat question, unlike supermarkets, because recipes and exact quantities arrive at your door.
alts: An internal sentence naming the target, its need, the category, the main benefit, the alternative and the proof that makes the claim believable.

cards.definition: A chart placing brands on two axes that matter to buyers (for example price and modernity) as customers perceive them. Empty zones can reveal an opportunity, or a place nobody wants.
cards.example: Placing car brands on cheap to premium and practical to sporty, to see where a new model could stand out.
alts: A two-axis chart showing where buyers place competing brands on criteria that matter to them, such as price and modernity.

cards.definition: Clayton Christensen idea: customers hire a product to get a job done in a given situation. Understanding the job explains choices better than demographics do.
cards.example: People buy a morning milkshake to make a boring commute more bearable and to stay full until lunch: its real competitors are bananas and bagels.
alts: The idea that customers hire an offer to make progress in a given situation, which reveals competitors that look nothing like you.

exercises.prompt: In what order does the STP method go?
exercises.explain: You cannot choose a target before splitting the market, and you cannot position yourself without knowing whose mind you want to win.

variants.prompt: Before choosing its targets and its positioning, what must a brand do?
Which step of STP answers: which customer groups do we choose to serve?

exercises.prompt: Splitting customers into heavy users and occasional buyers uses which type of criterion?
exercises.explain: Behavioural criteria describe what people do with the product: usage rate, loyalty, benefit sought, moment of purchase. They often predict buying better than age.

variants.prompt: Grouping customers by how often they order uses which type of criterion?
Which of these is a behavioural criterion?

exercises.prompt: Targeting people who value ecology and slow living uses which type of criterion?
exercises.explain: Values, attitudes and lifestyles are psychographic. Two 35-year-old Parisians with the same income can be very different on these.

variants.prompt: Targeting people who see themselves as adventurers and love risk uses which criterion?
Which of these is a psychographic criterion?

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT a condition of a good segment?
choices: Every member must be the same age
It is large enough to be profitable
You can reach it with your channels
exercises.explain: A segment groups people who react the same way to the offer. They do not need identical demographics.

variants.prompt: A segment must be measurable, large enough and reachable. What else?
choices: React differently from other segments to your offer
Have members who all live in the same city
Be chosen by the competitors first

variants.prompt: Left-handed golfers form a good segment. Why?
choices: They are measurable, reachable and need different gear
They all have the same age and income
They are the biggest group of golfers
They never compare prices before buying

exercises.prompt: A small brand serves only climbers, with a narrow but expert range. Which targeting strategy is it?
exercises.explain: Concentrated marketing (niche) lets a small player be the best for one group instead of average for everyone. The risk: depending on a single segment.

variants.prompt: A start-up makes software only for dental clinics. Which targeting strategy?
What is the main risk of a concentrated strategy?
choices: Spending too much on many segments
Having no clear positioning at all
Being too big for its niche

exercises.prompt: A carmaker sells a city car, a family SUV and a sports coupe, each with its own ads. Which strategy?
exercises.explain: Several segments, a specific offer and message for each: differentiated targeting. It reaches more people but costs more.

variants.prompt: A hotel group runs budget, mid-range and luxury brands, each with its own offer. Which strategy?
One product and one message for the whole market: which strategy?

exercises.prompt: Positioning is what you put in your ads; it exists as soon as the brand says it.
exercises.explain: False. Positioning is the place the brand occupies in the mind of the target. You can aim for it, but customers decide whether you got it.

variants.prompt: Positioning is the place a brand holds in the mind of its target, compared with its competitors.
variants.explain: True. You aim for it with the whole mix, but customers decide whether you got it.

variants.prompt: A new slogan is enough to change the positioning of a brand overnight.
variants.explain: False. Positioning lives in the minds of buyers and moves slowly, through product, price, distribution and years of consistent communication.

exercises.prompt: Which element is missing from this statement? For busy parents, Quitoque is the meal kit that removes daily menu planning.
choices: The alternative and the proof that make it credible
The founding date of the company
The list of all the recipes on offer
The colours of the brand logo
exercises.explain: A full positioning statement says unlike what, and why we can be believed. Without them, any competitor could write the same sentence.

variants.prompt: A statement reads: For runners, our shoe is the lightest. What does it lack?
choices: The alternative and the proof that make it credible
The founding date of the company
The list of all the shoe sizes
The colours of the brand logo

variants.prompt: Which part of a positioning statement answers: why should they believe it?

exercises.prompt: On a perceptual map, you find an empty zone: very cheap and very luxurious. What should you conclude?
choices: It may be empty because no real demand exists there
It is always a goldmine to occupy at once
The map was drawn the wrong way round
Competitors are hiding products in that zone
exercises.explain: A gap is a question, not an answer. Check that buyers actually want that combination before launching into it.

variants.prompt: A perceptual map shows no brand in the zone very cheap and very eco-friendly. What do you do first?
choices: Check that buyers want it and that it can pay off
Launch a product there at once
Redraw the map until the gap disappears
Copy the leader of the closest zone

variants.prompt: What does a perceptual map show?
choices: How buyers see brands on two axes that matter to them
The sales of each brand by region
The prices brands paid for their ads
The legal status of each competitor

exercises.prompt: Jobs to be done says people buy a morning milkshake to survive a boring commute. What does it change for the marketer?
choices: The real competitors become bananas, bagels and coffee
The target must be redefined by age and income
The price must be cut to match other drinks
Nothing: it only applies to software products
exercises.explain: The job reveals the real competition and the real benefits to improve: thicker, longer to drink, easy with one hand.

variants.prompt: People hire a power drill to get a hole in the wall. What does jobs to be done suggest?
choices: Compete on the result people want, not only on drills
Lower the price of the drill below all rivals
Add more features to the drill

variants.prompt: What does jobs to be done mainly look at to explain choices?
choices: The job the customer wants done in a situation
The age and income of the customer
The colour preferences of the customer
The advertising budget of the brand

exercises.prompt: Put the STP steps in order for a new vegan cheese brand.
steps: Split the market: flexitarians, vegans, lactose intolerant people
Assess each group: size, growth, reachability, fit with the brand
Choose flexitarians who want taste first as the main target
Define the place to win: the vegan cheese you serve to guests
Build the mix and the messages that prove this positioning
exercises.explain: Segment, evaluate, target, position, then execute. Most failed launches skip the evaluation and target everyone.
